paras: The lynching of Robert Robertson was the hanging of a Black private of the Twenty-fifth Infantry by masked men at Sun River, Montana Territory, about midnight on June 10–11, 1888. Robertson, called Robinson in many reports, was accused of fatally shooting Charles McGuire, a Sun River freighter, and was taken from a deputy at the Sun River jail. A judge sitting at Great Falls charged the grand jury against the lynchers, whom the grand jury could not identify.

Robertson's company had recently come to Fort Shaw from Fort Sisseton, Dakota, and a woman known as Queeny or Queenie Montgomery followed him and settled at Sun River. He and Matchett, a white private of the Third Infantry, were reported rivals for her, and the Tribune said that on Saturday, June 9, Robertson found Matchett at her house and beat him.

According to all the accounts, later that night Robertson shot McGuire (spelled Maguire in several Montana papers) in the forehead, killing him instantly. He fled to Fort Shaw and was arrested at the post, and on Sunday Sheriff Downing and Deputy Jack Hurley lodged him in the Sun River jail. A Cascade dispatch to the Helena Herald said cowboys were organizing to lynch him, and Downing telegraphed Judge Bach, who set out with two deputies to prevent violence.

About midnight a party of armed, masked men, fifty in most reports, came to the jail. In the Great Falls Tribune's account they demanded the key from Hurley, broke down the cell door, and hanged Robertson from a beam in a neighboring yard. The Fort Benton River Press said instead that they held Hurley at gunpoint and used a skeleton key, and that Downing found the body on a tree behind the stone store about 1 a.m. Judge Bach arrived after the hanging.

Judge W. P. Burcher, acting as coroner, held an inquest the next morning, and no one could be found who knew who did the lynching. In court on Monday, Judge Bach specially charged the grand jury against the lynchers, and the St. Paul Globe said he exonerated the sheriff. The grand jury later reported that its efforts to find the lynchers were "to no avail" and asked for an under sheriff at Sun River; no indictment or trial was reported. McGuire left a wife and two small children.

Outside Montana the story ran as a two-sentence Helena wire brief calling Robertson "a negro soldier" who killed "an innocent bystander" in a row over a woman. The New York Sun headed it "Lynched a Colored Soldier" on June 12, and the Indianapolis Journal and Narragansett Herald carried it among news briefs. Longer Helena dispatches in the Waterbury Evening Democrat, one headed "Shot the Wrong Man," stressed that McGuire was a bystander.

Montana papers framed the hanging as retribution. The St. Paul Globe's Great Falls special, titled "A Mob Metes Out Summary Justice to a Negro Murderer," predicted that it would check disturbances by "Uncle Sam's colored boys." The Tribune's narrative, reprinted by the Helena Weekly Herald and the Fergus County Argus, called the hanging a "weird, awe-inspiring scene" and closed, "Public vengeance was satisfied."

In an editorial the same day, the Tribune offered no sympathy for Robinson but argued that it would have been better to let the law take its course, since lynching discredited Montana among eastern settlers and investors. The River Press quoted McGuire as saying "Let's go and see what the coon looks like" and ended its account with "Comments are unnecessary."

Accounts differ on why McGuire was shot. Helena and Livingston dispatches said Robertson mistook him for Matchett; the Tribune said he fired after McGuire clapped and proposed to see the fun; the Herald's Cascade special said he fired at the nearest man in a crowd of white men. Reports also vary on the soldier's name (Robertson, Robinson, William Robinson), his weapon, and whether he was hanged from a tree or a beam. An Anaconda dispatch said he was lynched while being moved to Great Falls, a version the local accounts do not support.
